<meta>This page contains the "Summa Privilegii" (Summary of the Privilege), providing the legal authorization and copyright protection for the edition described on the preceding title page. It establishes the exclusive rights of the printer Denis du Val to produce this specific scholarly compilation of Emperor Julian's works.</meta>

## SUMMARY OF THE PRIVILEGE. <note>original Latin: "Summa Privilegii". A "privilege" was a royal grant of exclusive rights, functioning as an early form of copyright.</note>

By Royal Authority it is decreed that no one may print the works of the *Emperor Julian*, in Greek and Latin <note>original: "græ. lat."</note>, as edited by *Pierre Martin of Morentin in Navarre*, *Charles de Chanteclair, Royal Councilor and Master of Requests in the court, and Théodore Marcile*, or sell them elsewhere if printed outside this kingdom: except for *Denis du Val, bookseller and printer of the University of Paris*, for the nine-year period <note>original: "novennium"</note> following the completion of the edition. Whoever shall do otherwise will be punished by the confiscation of the books and by the penalties declared in the Royal decree. Given at Paris, the sixteenth of December, 1580.

->By decision of the council.<-

->Signed.<-

->BOURSIN.<- <note>Likely the name of the royal secretary or clerk who signed the patent.</note>

<summary>This page outlines the legal copyright granted by the French crown to the printer Denis du Val, giving him a nine-year monopoly on this specific edition of Emperor Julian's works. It names the contributing scholars and establishes the legal penalties for piracy or unauthorized sales.</summary>

<meta>Following the legal notice of the King’s privilege, this page begins the formal dedication of the work. The editor, Pierre Martin, addresses his patron, Cardinal Odet de Coligny, justifying the publication of works by a "pagan" emperor within a Christian society.</meta>

<header>TO OTHO II <note>Odet de Coligny (1517–1571), a high-ranking French prelate and brother of the Huguenot leader Gaspard de Coligny. Odet famously converted to Protestantism while retaining his title as Cardinal.</note></header>

# TO COLIGNY
## CARDINAL OF CHÂTILLON
## PIERRE MARTIN
### of Morentin in Navarre, sends greetings.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'S' featuring leafy scrollwork and architectural motifs.</image-desc>

I TRULY hope (most noble Cardinal) that no one will be justly angry with me if I publish the works <note>original Latin: "monumenta," literally 'monuments' or 'records'</note> of the Emperor Julian for the public. For while I grant that the crimes of impiety and tyranny, in which that wretched man miserably entangled himself, are wicked and worthy of hatred; yet certainly the most brilliant lights of his eloquence and genius do not deserve, I believe, to be extinguished along with his sins. Otherwise, let Demosthenes, Cicero, Homer, Virgil, Plato, Aristotle, and in a word all the authors of elegant and refined literature—poets, orators, philosophers—be removed from our midst; finally, let all the arts of humanity and wisdom be removed, because they were mostly handed down by superstitious or impious men. If that were to happen, what kind of republic, I ask, would we hold today? But among the Latins, Lucretius, and among the Greeks, Porphyry and Lucian are read in Greek and Latin editions: and yet I believe there is no one who complains that their works exist. For it is primarily relevant to the value of history and the knowledge of antiquity, not only that those men once lived, but also to know who and what kind of people they were. But you may say they were impious. So be it, since the examples of these men are effective for deterring people and calling them back from impiety; hence that unhappy Theseus cries out in the underworld as an example of his own misery, as it is written in Virgil’s *Aeneid*, Book 6:

> Learn justice, be warned, and do not slight the gods. <note>original Latin: "Discite justitiam moniti, & non temnere divos." This is a famous line from Virgil describing the eternal punishment of the wicked.</note>

Moreover, the history of Julian is worthy of a certain special attention and observation. In him were exceptional gifts of nature and talent, great virtue and nearly singular skill in administering the affairs of war and peace; to these many good qualities was added the knowledge of true piety <note>Julian was raised as a Christian before his "apostasy" or return to paganism.</note>, adorned even by ample testimonies of his life. But the man, burning with a desire for power, and captured by the deceits and arts of magic, renounced Christ; and having attained the power of the highest command, he most cruelly harassed the Christians, banned them from schools, removed them from magistracies, despoiled them of their goods, expelled Athanasius <note>St. Athanasius of Alexandria, a leading figure in early Christianity and a fierce opponent of Julian.</note>, and finally in all ways disturbed and afflicted the Church. It will therefore be useful to recall from these records both what the state of those times was and what the feelings of good men were.

<sig>A ij</sig> <note>This is a signature mark, used by early printers to help binders assemble the pages of a book in the correct order.</note>

<summary>This dedication by Pierre Martin to Cardinal Odet de Coligny defends the scholarly publication of the Emperor Julian’s writings. Martin argues that Julian’s literary and intellectual merits should be studied despite his historical role as a persecutor of Christianity.</summary>

<keywords>Julian the Apostate, Odet de Coligny, Pierre Martin, humanism, classical education, religious history, Athanasius, Virgil, ancient philosophy</keywords>

--- Page 6 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedication to Cardinal Odet de Coligny. Having argued that the works of the "apostate" Emperor Julian should be preserved for their historical and literary value despite his religious failures, Martin now compares the reading of these texts to the relief felt by a victor surveying a defeated enemy’s camp.</meta>

<header>EPISTLE.</header>

Truly, what a great joy it will be for the Church, having finally endured and been freed from such great evils, not only to remember her past labors, but also to look upon the enemies by whom she was so often wounded now driven out, their camps deserted, and their leader cast down and lying defeated? In this same way, the Trojans, exhausted by the weariness of their long siege, rejoiced when they saw the enemy had moved away, as the same poet <note>The "poet" is Virgil, the most famous of the Roman epic poets.</note> says in the second book of the *Aeneid*:

> Therefore all Troy releases itself from long grief:
> The gates are opened; it is a joy to go and see the Greek camps,
> The deserted places, and the abandoned shore:
> Here the troop of Dolopians <note>A group of Greek warriors from Thessaly.</note> stayed, here fierce Achilles used to pitch his tent.

Therefore, this pleasure in reading these texts will be added to the practical utility of history. For this reason, even if no eloquence or charm of genius appeared in these writings, no one, I believe, should take it poorly that these benefits of utility and pleasure have been shared with them through our efforts.

As for the reliability of this edition, I obtained a single manuscript copy from the library of Pierre Ramus <note>Pierre de la Ramée (1515–1572), a famous French humanist, logician, and Martin’s teacher.</note>. Because that copy was faulty in several places, we have changed the old reading where it seemed to be in error according to our best judgment; however, we have provided notes <margin>how it was read previously</margin> to show how the text appeared before our corrections.

You will receive, therefore (most distinguished Cardinal), both this modest gift of an edition and myself, its author, with that kindness with which you are accustomed to receive all those in whom some sign of virtue and good will appears. Your honors are many and illustrious in every field, but one in particular will be praised and carried to the heavens as long as literature exists: that you protect, adorn, and enlarge the Academy of Paris; that by your generosity you support the studies of many; and finally, that you embrace good and learned men with singular zeal and love.

Because you hold Pierre Ramus, my teacher, in such high esteem, I say that you bind not only me but all people throughout the world who love true education—and who have been awakened and helped by his late-night labors—to yourself forever. You draw them to love you and to serve you with every duty. I also have several other works, including a Hebrew grammar we have developed using logical principles <note>Martin is referring to "Ramist" logic, a method of organizing knowledge into diagrams and definitions.</note>, which will soon be published in your name if I learn that these current efforts have not been unwelcome to you. Farewell. Paris <note>Original Latin: "Lutetiae," the Roman name for Paris.</note>, the first of May, 1566.

->P. MARTIN<-

<summary>Pierre Martin concludes his dedication to Cardinal de Coligny by explaining his editorial process using Pierre Ramus's library and praising the Cardinal's patronage of the University of Paris. He also announces a forthcoming Hebrew grammar book organized according to Ramist logic.</summary>

# PIERRE MARTIN
## OF MORENTIN IN NAVARRE
### PREFACE TO JULIAN’S

->*The Emperor’s Misopogon <note>The title translates to "Beard-Hater." It is a satirical work written by Julian in 363 AD against the citizens of Antioch who had mocked his appearance and his austere, philosophical lifestyle.</note>, in which the*<-
->*author’s life is discussed, drawn from various*<-
->*sources, especially the writings*<-
->*of Marcellinus <note>Ammianus Marcellinus (c. 330–397 AD), a Roman soldier and historian who served under Julian and is the primary historical source for his reign.</note>.*<-

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'J' decorated with stylized vine scrolls and a central fleur-de-lis motif.</image-desc>JULIAN THE EMPEROR possessed such singular talent and eloquence that his surviving works clearly demonstrate it. Even in the records of history, he is granted no small praise for other virtues worthy of a ruler, so much so that, if the things recorded about him are true, I would not hesitate to compare him in those respects to the very greatest of princes. However, the single stain of his impiety and <term>apostasy</term> <note>original: ἀποστασίας (*apostasias*). This refers to Julian’s rejection of Christianity in favor of a return to Roman paganism, which earned him the historical epithet "Julian the Apostate."</note> has forever erased and extinguished all those praises. 

This serves as a great example and must be considered above all else, so that both princes and private citizens might dread the danger of such a vast and wretched ruin. They should realize that the Best and Greatest God must be worshipped sincerely, and that they must embrace true piety truly and seriously, not thinking it to be some childish game or joke. They must reflect upon that most certain oracle of Christ: <term>“Many are called, but few are chosen,”</term> <note>original: πολλοὶ εἰσὶν κλητοὶ, ὀλίγοι δὲ ἐκλεκτοὶ (*polloi eisin klētoi, oligoi de eklektoi*); see Matthew 22:14.</note>. 

Therefore, so that this entire matter may be more easily understood, and the argument of the following speech be explained through its causes, we must first learn of Julian’s life from his nature and upbringing, and then from his character. Nature involves his homeland and parents, as well as his natural mental and physical disposition. His homeland, then, was Byzantium <note>The ancient Greek city on the Bosporus which became the capital of the Eastern Roman Empire.</note>, a noble and wealthy city of Thrace and then the seat and home of the empire, which was later called Constantinople and New Rome. His parents were no less noble and famous than his homeland. For his father was Constantius <note>Julius Constantius, the half-brother of Constantine the Great.</note>, the brother of that great Constantine, and his mother was named Basilina, who was already noble by her ancestry, as Marcellinus says; to whom, however, not

He begins a biographical sketch of Julian, noting his noble lineage and his birth in Byzantium (Constantinople).</summary>

->PREFACE<-

<meta>The previous page ended with "They should realize that the Best and Greatest God must be ...". This page picks up with the following:</meta>

...worshipped above all, so that he might have been able to enjoy much. For indeed, after the death of his brother Constantine <note>Constantine II, who died in 340 AD.</note>, Julian’s father was crushed by the successors of the empire; his mother, however, departed this life only a few months after Julian was born. Thus, while still quite a young boy, he was left destitute of all hope of comfort or protection, along with his brother Gallus—his only paternal sibling—who was himself of fragile and nearly broken health. Indeed, the same ruin that had previously overtaken their father would have crushed both sons as well, had not Julian’s youth and Gallus’s ill health spared them from the immediate danger.

These, then, were the seeds of his nature sown amidst the splendor of his lineage and parentage. Yet, in his mind and body, nature’s disposition was quite varied. His mind was indeed most volatile; thus (as Marcellinus <note>Ammianus Marcellinus, the Roman historian.</note> states in Book 22), he allowed his prefects and associates to confidently restrain his impulses with timely admonition whenever they strayed further than was proper; he frequently demonstrated that he grieved for his errors and took joy in being corrected. 

The modest build of his body is described by the same author in his twenty-fifth book: *“His physical frame,”* he says, *“was as follows: he was of medium height, with hair that was soft, looking as though it had been combed, and a shaggy beard tapering to a point. He possessed eyes of a flashing beauty that betrayed the restless intensity* <note>original: *angustias*—literally "narrowness" or "straits," here referring to a crowded, anxious, or shifty state of mind.</note> *of his mind. He had handsome eyebrows and a perfectly straight nose, a slightly large mouth with a cleft lower lip, and a thick, arched neck with broad, powerful shoulders. From his head to the very tips of his toes, the alignment of his frame was straight and well-knit, giving him great strength and speed in running.”* 

In this mention of "restless intensity," the same volatility noted above is observed; however, to this is added a physical hardiness, from which a great measure of his subsequent military glory was derived.

Yet on this entire subject, the discourse of Gregory of Nazianzus <note>A prominent 4th-century Christian theologian who studied with Julian in Athens.</note> is more detailed and outspoken. He encountered Julian as a young man in Athens and, from the disposition of his mind and body, foresaw his future character. Thus he speaks in his second book *Against Julian*: *“At that time,”* he says, *“I realized I was no poor judge of character, even though I am not naturally gifted in those arts of divination. But it was his mental instability and extraordinary agitation that made me capable of foresight—for indeed, the best prophet is one who knows how to guess correctly* <note>This is a Latin rendering of a Greek proverb: "The best seer is he who guesses well."</note>. *It seemed to me no sign of anything good to see that bowed neck, those twitching and shrugging shoulders, a wandering eye that rolled with a wild gaze, feet that were unstable and stumbling, and a mocking expression that breathed forth contempt and...”*

->ON JULIAN’S *MISOPOGON* <note>The *Misopogon* (Beard-Hater) is a satirical essay written by Emperor Julian himself to mock the citizens of Antioch who had ridiculed his appearance and ascetic lifestyle.</note><-

...contempt, ridiculous facial expressions, the same kind of unrestrained and excessive laughter, irrational nodding and shaking of the head, a hesitant speech broken by breaths, silly and foolish questions, and answers no better than those, colliding into one another, inconsistent, and not following a scholarly order. Why should I list each one? I saw him as such before his works, as I came to know him in his works. These are his words, from which we understand the perpetual levity and inconstancy implanted and innate in this man, so that the primary cause of the error that followed is already grasped. Therefore, such was his nature.

What of his education, by what masters, and by what kind of studies and arts was it handled and cultivated? After his seventh year of age, he was handed over to the tutor Mardonius the eunuch, regarding which he himself addresses the people of Antioch in the *Misopogon* in this manner: "Do you wish (he says) for me to bring forth the name and race of my pedagogue? He was a barbarian and a Scythian by race, of the same name as he <note>Mardonius was the name of the Persian general who persuaded Xerxes to invade Greece in 480 BCE.</note> who led Xerxes to war in Greece and to noble Argos. This name, however, which before my twentieth year was used out of honor, is now used as a slur. He was a Eunuch, educated under my grandfather, to explain the poems of Homer and Hesiod to my mother. Since she died a few months later, having left me as her first and only son, I was then like an orphaned and deserted maiden, rescued from many calamities, a girl and tender [child], and after my seventh year, I was handed over to him." 

From this teacher, therefore, he was led to the public schools in Constantinople, and there he spent his childhood years in grammatical and rhetorical studies: he had Nicocles the Lacedæmonian <term>Lacedæmonian: another name for a Spartan.</term> as his master of the art of grammar, and Ecebolius the sophist as his master of rhetoric. 

<margin>About Ecebolius</margin>
Furthermore, this master later followed the fortune of his pupil and defected from the Christians to the pagans <term>ethnicos: literally "the nations," a common term for non-Christians or pagans.</term>, and finally, after Julian’s death, having returned to the Christians, he lay prostrate before the doors of the temple shouting, "Trample upon me, the tasteless salt." <note>original: "Calcate me salem insipidum." This is a reference to the Gospel of Matthew 5:13, where salt that loses its flavor is fit only to be trampled underfoot.</note> Nevertheless, for Julian, this school was no less a school of piety and religion than of intellect and letters. Thus, he performed the public office of a reader <term>anagnostæ: a minor clerical rank in the early church responsible for reading scripture aloud during the liturgy.</term> in the church and recited the sacred books in the hearing of the people; nor did he think that anything greater or more abundant could happen to him for his glory than piety. Therefore, devoted to these masters and arts, he briefly achieved such fame and authority among all that...

A iiij

<meta>This page continues the biography of Julian the Apostate, picking up from the description of his early education under the eunuch Mardonius. It describes his move to Nicomedia and his intellectual transition from Christian studies to pagan rhetoric and Neoplatonic philosophy under the influence of Libanius and Iamblichus.</meta>

<page-num>16</page-num>
<header>PREFACE</header>

...it was frequently said that he was fit for governing the empire. And so, lest any occasion for revolution might arise from that reputation, he departed from this first school for Nicomedia. 

<margin>Libanius the Rhetorician</margin>
Libanius the Rhetorician <note>Libanius (c. 314–393 AD) was one of the most famous teachers of rhetoric in the later Roman Empire and a lifelong friend of Julian.</note> was flourishing in that city at the time, held in great praise for his eloquence, but he was particularly devoted to pagan superstition. For this reason, Julian at first kept away from his school and only read his books at home, because he was wonderfully delighted by them. But later, gradually corrupted by familiarity with Libanius, he began not only to frequent the school but even dared, after the Greek fashion, to declaim against Christians, as if for the sake of exercising his talent he wanted to make some incredible thesis seem plausible through speaking. This was Julian’s second school: a school, I say, the mistress of error and impiety. Indeed, the Apostle Paul rightly says, quoting the poet Menander:

> “Bad company corrupts good character.” <note>original Greek: Φθείρουσιν ἤθη χρηστὰ ὁμιλίαι κακαί; Latin: Corrumpunt mores bonos congressus mali. This is a quote from the playwright Menander, famously cited by St. Paul in 1 Corinthians 15:33.</note>

Nevertheless, in this school, such were his exercises in eloquence. There he also learned philosophy. At that time, philosophy was not entirely Platonic or Aristotelian, but a mixture of both; Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus, known for his anti-Christian writings.</note> a little before, and Iamblichus then, were considered the leaders of this school.

<margin>Iamblichus, the greatest philosopher</margin>
Iamblichus held the highest authority among all: thus, Julian especially cultivated and loved this philosopher, bestowing great honors and rewards upon him. He held philosophy of this sort: hence in his letters he calls himself "a zealot for the doctrines of Plato and Aristotle" <note>original Greek: τῶν πλάτωνος καὶ ἀριστοτέλους ζηλωτὴν δογμάτων</note>. In this matter, he also made much use of the labor of that eunuch teacher I mentioned before, just as he himself declares to the people of Antioch in the *Misopogon* <note>The "Beard-Hater," Julian's satirical defense of his lifestyle.</note>, when he shifts the blame for his life upon him with a certain irony. "Often (he says) these names, I believe, have been heard—so much, clearly, have they been criticized and mocked—Plato, Socrates, Aristotle, Theophrastus. When that old man [Mardonius] had followed them with excessive folly and simplicity, and later finding me as a boy burning with the desire for learning, he persuaded me that if I wished to follow in their footsteps, I would become a better man—perhaps not better than other men (for there was no competition between me and them), but certainly better than my former self. But I (for what else could I have done?), having obeyed the old man, can no longer change anything, however much I might desire it; and I reproach myself for [giving in to] all..."

<meta>catchword: all</meta>

The author characterizes this shift as a descent into error and impiety, influenced by both his tutors and classical Greek philosophy.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the biography of the Emperor Julian, specifically his shift from the influence of his early tutor Mardonius to the more controversial influence of the Neoplatonist Maximus of Ephesus. The previous page ended with a discussion of his early training in Nicomedia.</meta>

<page-num>17</page-num>
<header>ON JULIAN’S MISOPOGON <note>The "Misopogon" (Beard-Hater) was a satirical work written by Julian himself.</note></header>

...boundaries, <note>The word "terminibus" (boundaries/limits) is completed here from the previous page's catchword "ter-".</note> I shall not provide a free entrance for vices. But those things which the Athenian Guest <note>The "Athenian Guest" is the primary speaker in Plato's *Laws*.</note> discusses in the works of Plato come to mind:

> He is worthy of honor who commits no sin; but he who even deters others from injury is worthy of more than double honor. For the former is equal to one man, while the latter is equal to many, as he reports the crime of others to the magistrates; but he who, moreover, offers himself as an ally in punishing the injury, this man is great and perfect in the state, and let him be declared the victor in the contest of virtue. <note>original Latin: Dignus est honore, qui nihil peccat... This is a translation of Plato's Laws, Book V, 730d.</note>

That old man <note>Referring to Mardonius, Julian's childhood tutor.</note> used to teach me these things. And such was Julian's philosophy until now. Meanwhile, Maximus of Ephesus, the philosopher, came to Nicomedia. 

<margin>Maximus of Ephesus, philosopher</margin>
Maximus of Ephesus was a philosopher who, on account of his magical arts and impostures, was later punished by the Emperor Valentinian <note>Valentinian I, Roman Emperor from 364–375 AD.</note> with the death penalty. He was Julian's second corrupter, and he taught him, as Nazianzen <note>St. Gregory of Nazianzus (c. 329–390 AD).</note> says, "all the impiety that deals in the marvels of astronomy, horoscopes, and the illusion of foreknowledge, and the sorcery that follows these," <note>original Greek: ὅσην τε περὶ ἀστρονομίαν καὶ τὰς γενέσεις καὶ φαντασίαν προγνώσεως τερατεύεται, καὶ τὴν ἑπομένην τούτοις γοητικήν.</note> which plays at both astronomy and natal charts and the appearance of divination, and the magic that accompanies them. How highly Julian always valued this philosopher is declared by the letters written to him in such honorable words. From this school, he then moved to Athens "for the sake of exploring Greece and its schools of learning," <note>original Greek: καθ’ ἱστορίαν τῆς ἑλλάδος, καὶ τῶν ἐκεῖσε παιδευτηρίων.</note> to visit Greece and get to know the schools of that region, says Gregory, where we noted above that Julian became known to him. 

Therefore, Julian's doctrine was established by such teachers and arts, so that from this point, the second cause of his error easily appears. And yet, so far we see only the seeds, both of his nature and his education; let us next see the fruits in his character. Marcellinus, <note>Ammianus Marcellinus (c. 330–400 AD), a Roman soldier and historian.</note> in Book 14, touches upon them generally when he compares the character of Julian's brother, Gallus. He says: "Julian differed as much from the temperate character of his brother as Domitian was from Titus among the sons of Vespasian." Here, Gallus is compared to Domitian, and Julian to Titus. <note>Titus was remembered as a "good" emperor, while his brother Domitian was remembered as a tyrant.</note> And indeed, Julian seems not to have been averse to moderation and modesty of mind, since among all the emperors he especially loved the philosopher Marcus [Aurelius] and proposed him as his model to imitate. This fruit was certainly not so much of nature as of education, which, as Ovid says:

-> It softens the spirit and does not allow it to be wild. <-

# PREFACE

...[this third] cause, joined to those two former ones of which we spoke before regarding nature and education, might easily lead a man away from truth and right and plunge him into fraud and crime. Nevertheless, let us now look at his character in each aspect of the virtues. And first, of what kind was his courage? As a young man not yet past his twenty-third year, he was created Caesar <note>In this period of the Roman Empire, 'Caesar' was the title for the junior emperor or heir-apparent, serving under the senior 'Augustus.'</note> on the sixth of November during the consulship of Arbetio and Lolliano, at a time when barbarians were wasting the Gallic provinces and the Emperor was prevented by fear from waging war against them.

Constantius (says Marcellinus <note>Ammianus Marcellinus, a 4th-century historian and soldier who is a primary source for Julian's life.</note> in book 15) was troubled by constant reports indicating that Gaul was in a desperate state, with no one resisting while the barbarians laid waste to everything until the point of total extermination. Shaking for a long time over how he might repel these calamities while residing in Italy himself (as he desired—for he considered it dangerous to thrust himself into a region so far removed), he finally found a proper plan. He thought to admit his paternal cousin Julian—who had not long ago been brought back from Achaia by summons, and was even then still wearing the philosopher’s cloak <note>original: "palliatum." The *pallium* was the traditional cloak of scholars and philosophers, signaling Julian’s preference for study over military or courtly life.</note>—into a partnership of imperial power. And this he later accomplished, and furthermore gave him his sister Helena in marriage.

Julian, meanwhile, not unaware of the great dangers to which he was being exposed, considered himself called not so much to honor as to death. Therefore, on the day when, dressed in the royal purple and carried into the court in the imperial manner, he is said to have quoted this verse from Homer:

->*“Purple death and violent fate seized him.”*<-
<note>original Greek: *ἔλλαβε πορφύρεος θάνατος καὶ μοῖρα κραταιή.* This is a quote from the Iliad (5.83). Julian uses a pun here: "purple" refers both to the blood of a dying warrior and the color of the imperial robes he was forced to wear.</note>

He was also often heard murmuring that he had achieved nothing more than the "privilege" of dying while being busier than before. Hence that silent complaint in his work *The Beard-Hater* <note>original: *Misopogon*, a satirical essay written by Julian.</note> that he was relegated to the Gauls, the Germans, and the Hercynian Forest <note>A vast ancient forest in southern and central Germany.</note> so that he might wage war with wild beasts like a hunter. 

And in another place: "It seemed," he says, "that neither of us wished for it: neither he who gave this honor (or favor, or whatever other name you wish to call it) gave it willingly; and he who received it (the gods are witnesses) truly and from his soul refused it." These things he says about himself. And certainly (says Marcellinus), that rumor was tossed about everywhere: that Julian had been chosen not to relieve the troubles of Gaul, but so that he might be destroyed through most savage wars, since he was even then estimated to be unskilled—someone who would not likely endure even the sound of arms. Nevertheless, that "unskilled" youth, and student in the Academy...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Julian's transition from a scholar to a military leader. The text picks up from the previous page's discussion of his education in the "Academy" (the schools of philosophy in Athens) and his unexpected appointment as Caesar.</meta>

# ON JULIAN'S *MISOPOGON* <note>The "Beard-Hater," a satirical work written by Julian himself.</note>

...the shadow of the Academy, not raised in the sun and military dust, and yet, cast into such waves of great danger, what did he do? If he had merely wished to protect the province entrusted to him and repel injury without provoking the enemy, he would still be rightly judged to have performed a great feat. But he did provoke them, and he forced the one who was accustomed to being a terror to others to fear for himself. I say nothing of the speed with which he expelled the barbarians from Gaul, or the courage with which he defended the noble and ancient cities of Autun, Auxerre, Troyes, and Reims; finally, I make no mention of his other deeds in Gaul and Germany. I say only this, which all writers of that age proclaim with one voice: that seven of the most powerful kings of all Germany were defeated by him in a single massive and most difficult battle at Strasbourg <note>The Battle of Argentoratum in 357 AD, where Julian won a decisive victory over the Alamanni.</note>, and their prince Chonodomarius was captured and sent to Constantius at Rome, and the affairs of Gaul, which were entirely cut down and afflicted, were restored by him to a whole state. 

But even this praise was contaminated by the wretched stain of ambition when he wished to be hailed as Augustus <note>The title of senior Emperor. Julian was proclaimed Augustus by his troops in Paris, leading to a standoff with his cousin Constantius II.</note>: from which a most atrocious civil war would have followed, had not a nearly sudden death taken Constantius away beforehand. Upon receiving this news, Julian set out first for Constantinople to establish his rule, and then to Antioch for the Persian war. 

And here it should be noted what Socrates <note>Socrates Scholasticus, a 5th-century Christian church historian.</note> relates in his history: that Julian, persuaded by a certain Pythagorean <term>metempsychosis</term> <note>original: "μετεμψύχωσι" (metempsychosis) — the philosophical concept of the transmigration of souls, or reincarnation.</note>, believed himself to be Alexander the Great. Therefore, he perhaps hoped for similar glory from defeating the Persians; but the outcome was entirely different, as will be understood later. Wherefore we see that the great praise of this virtue truly shone forth in this emperor: let no one think that the study of letters and wisdom obstructs military glory, or that great things are managed by bodily strength more than by the prudence of the mind. 

But such was his courage; what of his temperance? It was truly admirable, both at home and abroad: and indeed his private temperance regarding food, sleep, and sex. Concerning food and sleep, Marcellinus writes in book 16: He forbade pheasant and sow's womb and udders <note>original: "Phasianum & vulvam & sumen." These were considered luxury delicacies in Roman dining which Julian rejected in favor of simple military rations.</note> to be demanded or served, content with the cheap and random food of a common soldier. From this it followed that he divided his nights into three parts for his duties: for rest, for public affairs, and for the Muses <note>Meaning his literary and philosophical studies.</note>; we read that Alexander the Great used to do this, but Julian did so much more strictly.

<margin>
Generally, in the writings of Marcellinus <note>Ammianus Marcellinus (c. 330–397 AD), a Roman soldier and historian who is the primary source for Julian's life.</note>, the words *xysira* and *Susurna* are incorrectly read.
</margin>
For that man <note>Likely referring to a historical figure like Alexander the Great, often cited as a model for light sleeping.</note>, by placing a bronze basin beneath him and holding a silver ball in his outstretched arm, ensured that when sleep relaxed the tension of his muscles, the ringing sound of the falling object would break his slumber. Julian, however, woke himself whenever he wished without any such device. Rising always at midnight, he did not emerge from feathers or silk blankets shimmering with uncertain light, but from a simple rug and a *sisyra* <note>original: σισύρᾳ; a coarse cloak or blanket made of shaggy goatskin.</note>, which common folk simply call a *Sisurna*. Julian himself declares this in his *Misopogon* <note>The "Beard-Hater," a work in which Julian satirizes himself and the people of Antioch.</note>, where he complains that he is hated by the people of Antioch for this very reason. "My private life," he says, "consisting of sleepless nights on a thin rug and a diet entirely lacking in richness, produces a harsh character that is at odds with this delicate city. Yet do not think this is done for your sake; a certain heavy and foolish error has led me since childhood to wage war upon my belly. For I do not allow it to be filled with feasts. Thus, it has very rarely happened that I have needed to vomit, and I remember this happening only once since I was made Caesar—and even then, not from an excess of food, but by mere chance." Thus, in this manner, he almost boasts of his temperance in food and sleep.

Furthermore, there followed a temperance in matters of love, concerning which Marcellinus writes in Book 25: "First," he says, "he shone with such inviolate chastity that after the loss of his wife, he never again engaged in any sexual act." He lost his wife shortly after receiving the honor of the title Augustus, having previously lost an infant son in Gaul. Soon after, the same author adds: "In the full strength of his adulthood, he so cautiously avoided this stain that he could not even be accused by the servants of his private life of even a suspicion of any lust, as often happens." And in Book 24, when commemorating the spoils captured in the Persian War, he says: "Among the captive virgins, who were beautiful—as they are in Persia, where the beauty of women excels—he did not wish to touch or even see any of them. In this, he imitated Alexander and Africanus <note>Scipio Africanus, the Roman general famous for his self-restraint with captives.</note>, who avoided such things lest they be broken by desire, having proven themselves invincible against hardships everywhere." Indeed, he even expelled barbers and cooks as if they were the servants of luxury and intemperance. Marcellinus writes in Book 22: "It happened that a barber, ordered to come and trim the Emperor's hair, entered dressed in an ambitious and costly fashion. Seeing him, Julian was struck with amazement and said, 'I did not ask for a finance officer <note>original: *rationalem*; a high-ranking official in the Roman treasury. The barber was dressed so elegantly Julian mistook him for a wealthy bureaucrat.</note>, but for a barber to be summoned.'" When the man was asked what...

# ON JULIAN’S *MISOPOGON* <note>Julian’s satirical work, the "Beard-Hater," where he responds to the criticisms of the people of Antioch.</note>

When he asked [a palace official] what he gained from his trade, the man replied: twenty daily rations of food, and as many portions of fodder for pack animals (which are commonly called *capita* <term>capita: literally "heads," a technical term for a unit of animal feed in the Roman military and civil bureaucracy</term>), as well as a heavy annual salary, in addition to many lucrative petitions. Moved by this, Julian dismissed all such individuals, along with cooks and others like them who were accustomed to receiving almost the same, as being hardly necessary to him, giving them the power to go wherever they wished. Such was his restraint within his own household. Next follows his external restraint regarding theaters and games, of which there is also a kind of boast disguised as self-reproach in the *Misopogon*. "I keep myself," he says, "away from the theaters through total stupidity, nor do I admit the stage into the palace, except at the beginning of the year, out of a mental dullness, like a poor farmer paying a tax to a harsh master. Even then, when I have entered, I am more like a man who detests those games than one watching them." He says the same a little later: "Pay attention, for what I am about to say is even more strange and admirable. I have always hated the Chariot Races, just as those who are burdened by debt hate the forum. Therefore, I rarely come to them, only on the festivals of the gods, and even then I do not spend the whole day there as my cousin, my uncle, and my paternal brother <note>Julian is likely referring to his predecessors and relatives, such as the Emperor Constantius II and his brother Gallus Caesar.</note> used to do. Instead, having watched perhaps the sixth race, and that without great pleasure—indeed, by Hercules, with annoyance and disgust—I gladly depart." And he says that this was the fruit of his education alone. "My teacher taught me," he says, "when I went to my masters, to look at the ground and not the theater, and to value the mind in my head more highly. Often that teacher would say to me when I was a boy: 'Do not let yourself be led into theaters by the crowd of your peers, nor be held by any desire for such a spectacle. Do you seek Chariot Races? You will find them most elegantly described in Homer; take up the book and read. Do you hear of actors and dancers? Let them be; the young men among the Phaeacians <note>A mythical people in Homer's *Odyssey* known for their skill in dancing and seafaring.</note> dance more vigorously. You have there the lyre-player Phemius and the singer Demodocus. There are also in Homer many descriptions that are heard with greater pleasure than our shows are watched.'"

->*“So once in Delos, near Apollo’s sacred altars,”*<-
->*“I saw a tall palm tree rising from the green grass.”*<-

### PREFACE

...a certain loquacity and unseemly behavior was noted in him. When one day (says Marcellinus <note>Ammianus Marcellinus (c. 330–397 AD), a Roman soldier and historian who served under Julian and is our primary source for his reign.</note>) it was announced to him while he was hearing court cases that the philosopher Maximus <note>Maximus of Ephesus, a Neoplatonist philosopher and Julian's spiritual mentor, who was later executed under Emperor Valens.</note> had arrived from Asia, he leaped up in an unseemly manner. Forgetting his dignity, he ran out far from the vestibule, kissed him, and received him reverently before leading him back inside. Through this untimely display, he appeared to be an excessive seeker of empty glory. This levity was natural and innate to him, as has been shown before, and no amount of learning could remove it. 

But since we have observed his self-restraint, let us look at his wisdom in every branch of learning. His mind’s great thirst for study is proved by a letter to a certain Ecdicius, the Prefect of Egypt, in which he demands the books of George, the Bishop of Alexandria. "Some," he says, "delight in horses, others in birds, and some in wild beasts. But I, indeed, from childhood have burned with a desire for books." Isocrates says, *If you are a lover of learning, you will be a man of much learning* <note>original: "ἐὰν ᾖς φιλομαθὴς, ἔσῃ πολυμαθὴς"</note>. Therefore, this love of learning produced in Julian a great breadth of knowledge. 

What then of the liberal arts—Grammar, Rhetoric, and Logic—and how did they manifest in him? We have already seen his masters of Grammar and Rhetoric, arts which also included Logic. However, let us seek a clearer and more certain proof of his learning from his own writings. It is likely that during that period of leisure spent in schools and studies, before he attained the honor of being named Caesar, he wrote many things that have perished due to the ravages of time. Among these, only a few orations sent to Iamblichus are mentioned, as is clear from a certain letter to him. But after he entered public life, he pursued and refined these studies even more diligently. 

From these midnight labors, Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world.</note> records: 
* *The Caesars* (as they are called), 
* *On the Three Figures* <note>original: "περὶ τριῶν σχημάτων"</note>, 
* *The Saturnalia* <note>original: "κρόνια"</note>, 
* *The Origin of Evil according to the Unlearned* <note>original: "πόθεν τὰ πόθεν τὰ κακὰ κατὰ τοὺς ἐπαιδεύτους"</note>, 
* *To the Cynic Heraclius* <note>original: "πρὸς τὸν κύνα ἡράκληον." The word "Cynic" is derived from the Greek word for "dog" (*kyon*), which the author translates literally here.</note>, 
* *How to live as a Cynic* <note>original: "πῶς κυνιστέον"</note>. 

All of these works, as far as I know, have perished. However, certain orations survive in Venice, a *Symposium* is found somewhere in Italy, and likewise a *Hymn to the Sun*. ### BY THE EMPEROR JULIAN
#### On wine made from barley.

Who are you? From where do you come, Dionysus? By the true Bacchus,
I do not recognize you; I know only the son of Zeus.
That one smells of nectar, but you smell of a goat. Truly, the Celts,
in their poverty of grapes, fashioned you from ears of grain.
Therefore, one should call you "child of Demeter," not "child of Dionysus,"

In a certain letter to Oribasius <note>Oribasius was a Greek physician and the personal doctor to the Emperor Julian; he was instrumental in Julian's rise to the throne.</note>, he relates a dream of his concerning a twin tree, by which he signifies himself and Constantius <note>Constantius II, Julian’s cousin and the reigning Emperor, whose relationship with Julian was fraught with suspicion.</note>. -> "I saw something like this today: I thought a tall tree was planted in a large dining hall, which bent toward the ground, and another small, tender, and very flourishing one had grown at its roots. But when I drew closer, I saw the great tree prostrate on the ground, while the small one was upright, yet suspended above the earth. Seeing this, I cried out in distress, 'Alas, what a great tree, and yet there is a risk that the shoot grown with it might also perish.' Here, someone entirely unknown to me said, 'Observe carefully, and be of good cheer: for since the root remains in the ground, that small tree will remain and take firmer hold.'" <-

<meta>This page continues the analysis of Emperor Julian’s character and intellectual life, moving from his interest in omens and astrology to his complex and often contradictory religious identity. <page-num>25</page-num>
# ON JULIAN’S *MISOPOGON* <note>The *Misopogon* ("Beard-Hater") was a satirical work by Emperor Julian written in 363 AD, where he addressed the citizens of Antioch who had mocked his pagan devotion and his philosopher’s beard.</note>
### B

...he lapsed into a harmful theology. "Secretly," says Marcellinus <note>Ammianus Marcellinus (c. 330–400 AD) was a Roman soldier and historian whose primary work, the *Res Gestae*, provides a detailed account of Julian’s reign.</note>, "he offered prayers to Mercury; and so that he might entice everyone to his favor without hindrance, he feigned adherence to the Christian worship, from which he had already long since secretly defected. He was intent upon the secrets of soothsaying and auguries—known only to a few participants—and other practices which the worshippers of the gods have always performed." 

This simulation lasted for as long as Constantius lived; but upon his death, Julian plainly changed his religion and, in the meantime, craftily encouraged dissension among the people so that he might reign more securely. "When indeed," says the same author in his twenty-second book, "having abolished the things he feared, he noticed that he had free time to do what he wished, he laid open the secrets of his heart. By clearly defined decrees, he ordered the temples to be opened, victims to be brought to the altars, and the cult of the gods to be restored." 

Furthermore, to strengthen the effect of his arrangements, he invited the disagreeing leaders of the Christians, along with the divided common people, into the palace. He advised them that, having put their civil discords to rest, each man should serve his own religion fearlessly and without prohibition. He did this obstinately for this reason: so that as license increased their dissensions, he would not later have to fear a united populace. This religious policy, therefore, sufficiently declares the man's theology. 

In performing sacred rites, however, he was foolishly superstitious, and even ridiculous to the pagans themselves. "He was superstitious," says Marcellinus in Book 25, "more than a legitimate observer of sacred rites, slaughtering countless cattle without thrift, so that it was estimated that if he returned from the Parthians <note>The Parthian (or Sassanid) Empire was the great rival to Rome in the East. Julian died during his campaign against them in 363 AD.</note>, oxen would soon be lacking." He was similar to that Emperor Marcus <note>Marcus Aurelius, whom Julian greatly admired but who was also teased for his excessive sacrifices.</note>, against whom we have received this saying: "The white oxen say to Marcus Caesar: If you are victorious, we are finished." <note>original Greek: "οἱ λευκοὶ βόες Μάρκῳ τῷ καίσαρι· ἂν σὺ νικήσῃς, ἡμεῖς ἀπωλόμεθα"</note> 
<margin>The word *synikēsē* is incorrectly read in Marcellinus.</margin>

Indeed, how much he burned with hatred for the Christian religion is declared by the books he wrote and published against it. His theology was of such a kind. Yet, he is said to have held an excellent opinion regarding the excellence of the soul. From this comes that truly noble saying of his: "It is a disgrace for a wise man, since he possesses a soul, to seek praise from the body." 

And this concerns his <term>Prudence</term><note>Prudence (*prudentia*) in the classical sense refers to practical wisdom and the ability to govern.</note>; but what of his <term>Justice</term>? What was it like? He snatched the supreme power from Constantius; this was the height of injustice. Although he did not harass the Christians with the sword and open force like the other tyrants before him, he nevertheless miserably vexed them with most unjust and bitter laws. Two edicts against them are extant in his letters: one by which he forbids them from the schools; the other...

<summary>This page discusses Emperor Julian’s deceptive religious transition, his use of Christian infighting to secure his power, and his excessive, often mocked, devotion to pagan animal sacrifices. It also introduces his legal persecution of Christians, specifically his ban on them teaching in schools.</summary>

<page-num>26</page-num>

# PREFACE

...by which he snatched away their goods and fortunes. He even most wickedly mocked them, claiming that he did this "so that they might more easily journey into the kingdom of heaven" <note>original: "ἵνα εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τῶν οὐρανῶν εὐδώτερον πορευθῶσι"</note>. Marcellinus <note>Ammianus Marcellinus, the historian cited on the previous page.</note> mentions the former edict in his twenty-second book. "But that decree," he says, "was harsh and should be buried in eternal silence, because it forbade teachers of rhetoric and grammar, who were followers of the Christian rite, from teaching." Indeed, he also forbade them from military service and from holding public office, saying that the Gospel took away the power of the sword from them, as Socrates recorded in his *Ecclesiastical History* <note>Socrates Scholasticus (c. 380–439 AD) was a Christian historian whose work continued the history of the Church where Eusebius left off.</note>. In this, Julian perversely and maliciously usurped the authority of the Gospel, which does not forbid public justice, but rather private vengeance. He even rejected Christians who complained of injuries, mocking them with the phrase: "It is your lot to suffer injuries" <note>original: "ὑμέτερον τὸ κακοπαθεῖν"</note>.

Out of hatred for the Christians, he favored the Jews with benefits and encouraged them to restore their temple; regarding this matter, an edict exists among his letters. But the Jews attempted this in vain and to their great disadvantage, contrary to the decree of God. Marcellinus is a witness to this in his twenty-third book. "The once ambitious temple at Jerusalem," he says, "which after many deadly battles was conquered with difficulty by the siege of Vespasian and later Titus, Julian thought to restore with immoderate expense. He gave the task of speeding the business to Alypius of Antioch, who had formerly governed Britain as a deputy prefect. Therefore, when Alypius was vigorously pressing the work, and the governor of the province was assisting him, terrifying balls of flame broke out near the foundations with frequent attacks, making the place inaccessible to the workers, who were burned several times. In this way, with the element driving them back more resolutely, the undertaking ceased."

And he did not set aside this great hatred for Christians even in the settlement of legal cases; for he would ask which religion each of the litigants practiced. Yet within this unfairness of the emperor, a certain zeal for maintaining equity appeared, in that he reformed certain parts of the civil law. "He corrected the laws for the better," says Marcellinus in his twenty-second book, "cutting away ambiguities and clearly indicating what they ordered to be done or what they forbade."

<margin>He also hated informers; and so, when someone accused a wealthy citizen before Julian of treason, he turned to the Count of the Sacred Largesses <note>The *comes sacrarum largitionum* was the senior financial official of the later Roman Empire, responsible for the treasury and the mints.</note> and said, "Order that purple coverings for the feet <note>Purple footwear was a symbol of imperial rank. Julian is mockingly suggesting that the informer, by meddling in the affairs of the state, is acting as if he were the emperor himself.</note> be given to this man to be brought to his adversary."</margin>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Roman Emperor Julian (reigned 361–363 AD), specifically evaluating his character and his stay in Antioch. ### ON JULIAN’S *MISOPOGON*. <note>The *Misopogon*, or "Beard-Hater," was a satirical essay written by Emperor Julian to mock the people of Antioch who had ridiculed his appearance and lifestyle.</note>

When the orator Delphidius was fiercely accusing a certain man, and finally cried out in a lack of evidence, "O most flourishing Caesar, who will ever be able to be found guilty, if it is enough to simply deny the charge?" Julian responded, <margin>,,</margin> "Who will be able to be found innocent, if it is enough to have made an accusation?" <margin>,,</margin> I praise this fairness of mind in a prince; however, the events that follow have only the appearance of clemency. <margin>,,</margin> When he was preparing for war against Constantius <note>Constantius II, Julian's cousin and predecessor</note>, and all the soldiers agreed except for one man, Nebridius, for which reason Nebridius was placed in great danger, the Emperor covered him with his own military cloak <note>original Latin: "paludamento"</note>. And when that man, cast down and pleading, asked for the Emperor's right hand, Julian said: "What special distinction will be reserved for my friends, if you touch my hand?" <margin>,,</margin> Truly, when the prefect Lucillianus found himself in a nearly identical case, and the opportunity was given to him to adore the imperial purple <note>a ritual of submission and pardon</note>, he—now somewhat recovered from his fear—said: "O Emperor, you have committed yourself incautiously and rashly with so few men to the territory of your enemies." Julian replied with a smile: <margin>,,</margin> "Save these words of 'prudence' for Constantius; for I have extended the insignia of majesty to you not as a counselor, but so that you may cease to be afraid." <margin>,,</margin> Therefore, let this moderation and fairness of mind be praised thus far. But what follows would seem in no way worthy of a wise and political prince. For when he had departed from Constantinople and come to Antioch to wage war with the Persians, and decided to spend the winter in that city, he—led by no probable reason, but only by an empty desire for glory, so that he might seem a prince of the people—lowered the legal price of the grain supply <note>original: "annonæ"</note>. This matter brought famine and scarcity to the city, and produced the greatest hatred toward Julian. <margin>,,</margin> And as the people of Antioch were witty and sharp-tongued by a certain native freedom of character, they mocked Julian in various ways. <margin>,,</margin> Marcellinus <note>The historian Ammianus Marcellinus</note> says in Book 22: "He was laughed at as a *cercops* <note>A mischievous, monkey-like creature from mythology; original: "cercops"</note>, a short man, stretching out narrow shoulders and displaying a goat-like beard, walking with great strides as if he were the brother of Otus and Ephialtes <margin>,,</margin> <note>Two giants from Greek mythology who tried to storm heaven</note>, whose height Homer praises immensely." He was also called "The Slaughterer" <note>original: "Victimarius"</note> instead of "The Priest," with many people alluding to the frequency of his animal sacrifices; and he was appropriately blamed for this, since for the sake of ostentation he would freely carry the sacred objects instead of the priests, rejoicing in a retinue of low-born women. By these words of Marcellinus, two things are chiefly noted in Julian: his person and his religion. Let a third be added from the *Misopogon*, concerning the image on his coin. It was a bull... <margin>,,</margin>

### PREFACE

<margin>)</margin>
...an altar turned upward, by which Julian signified that the ancient custom of <margin>7/</margin> sacrifices had been restored by him: but the people of Antioch interpreted <margin>11</margin> it as the world being turned upside down by Julian. Therefore, to avenge insults of this kind, the *Misopogon* <note>The *Misopogon*, or "Beard-Hater," is a satirical work where Julian mocks himself to actually criticize the city of Antioch.</note> was published, the summary of which must now be briefly explained. In it, roughly three crimes are charged against the people of Antioch: the first is lack of self-control, because they are devoted to games and theaters; the second is impiety, because, having neglected the religion of their ancestors, <note>The following six words are underlined in the original</note> they worship Christ instead of Jupiter and Apollo; the third and last is the injustice of the magistrates, who tolerate and ignore the greed of the wealthy, from which a famine has arisen in the city. And although the people of Antioch are actually being rebuked in this oration, a contrary appearance is feigned: for indeed, a constant irony is employed in the Socratic manner <note>original Greek: σωκρατικῶς (*sōkratikōs*)</note>, by which Julian seems to accuse not the Antiochians, but himself, because he is unable to imitate their ways. For the people of Antioch are introduced, as if in a dialogue, discussing Julian’s beard (from which the work is called the *Misopogon* <note>original Greek: μισοπώγων (*misopōgōn*), literally "beard-hater"</note>) and indeed his entire person and life—that it is foreign to all pleasure, that it is too religious, and finally that it is too severe in legal judgments. Julian ironically confesses all these things to be his "crimes" and begs for pardon, shifting the blame onto his tutor, by whom he was taught from boyhood to live temperately, religiously, and justly; and then he claims he spent his youth among the Gauls, men who are harsh, warlike, and ignorant of luxuries. The sum of this reproach, therefore, is contained in this syllogism <note>A logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises.</note>:

> He who opposes the customs of others is deservedly accused by them:
> *Julian opposes the customs of the Antiochians, because he despises pleasures, and because he restrains the impiety and injustice which they strictly hold and defend:*
> *Therefore, he is deservedly accused by them.*

Finally, this ironic reproach is concluded with a serious reproach of this kind:

> *He who gives benefits to the ungrateful is a fool:*
> *Julian gave benefits to the ungrateful, since he praised, enriched, and supported the Antiochians before they were even known to him:*
> *Therefore, he is a fool.*

This is the summary of the entire speech, in which many things are false and irrelevant. For the charge of impiety against the Antiochians was made because they, having rejected the superstitions of their ancestors...

<meta>This page continues the analysis of Julian’s *Misopogon*, moving from a summary of its contents to a critique of Julian's historical accuracy and his motives for writing the satire, supported by quotes from the historian Ammianus Marcellinus and the theologian Gregory of Nazianzus.</meta>

### ON JULIAN’S *MISOPOGON*

...superstition, they had embraced the Christian religion, which Julian was most wickedly accustomed to call "godlessness." <note>original Greek: *atheotēta* (ἀθεότητα). Julian used this term because Christians refused to acknowledge the traditional Roman gods.</note> This, therefore, is a slander. As for what he says regarding luxuries, although there is some truth to it, the Christian religion had already corrected many such behaviors. Furthermore, the magistrates are blamed in vain for the city's famine and poverty, since Julian himself was the author of it.

This is confirmed even by Marcellinus <note>Ammianus Marcellinus (c. 330–397 AD) was a Roman historian who served under Julian and generally admired him, making his criticism here particularly significant.</note>, although he is otherwise full of praise for Julian, in Book 22: *“For no plausible reason,”* he says, *“but out of a desire for popularity, he was eager to lower the prices of goods for sale. This, when arranged in a way that is not appropriate, usually breeds scarcity and famine. Although the council of Antioch openly demonstrated that this could not be done at his command, he never turned aside from his purpose—resembling his brother Gallus <note>Gallus Caesar, Julian's elder half-brother, was known for a much more violent and erratic temperament.</note> in this regard, though he remained unstained by blood. Consequently, raging against them thereafter as detractors and stubborn people, he composed an invective volume which he called the 'Antiochian' or 'Misopogon,' counting the insults of the city with a hostile mind and adding many things to the truth.”*

These are the words of Marcellinus, from which we understand that rhetorical colors were employed in that speech to obscure the truth. Gregory of Nazianzus <note>A 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople and one of the "Cappadocian Fathers."</note> mentions this speech at the end of his second book against Julian in these words:

> This speech of yours is born from the lies and trifles of Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and famous critic of Christianity.</note>, in which you all exult as if they were divine voices, or rather from your *Misopogon* or *Antiochian* (for you give both titles to the work). What could be more dishonorable for Christians than this? At that time, your imperial purple made the work seem great, as did the sycophants who admired everything of yours. But now, it is a "beard" that is chattered about and dragged through the mud, laughed at by those who suffered along with you. In this work, you puff yourself up out of a greedy desire—because you were never able to satisfy the physical needs of your body—as if you were saying something wonderful. But you willingly pass over the fact that you drove out the Christians so bitterly and destroyed such a sacred and great nation. Indeed, if you merely jumped away from one man or let out natural belches, what harm does that do to the public? But when such a great persecution was set in motion and such a great confusion of innovation introduced, how is it not entirely necessary for the affairs of the Romans to be in a bad state?

That is to say: This speech of yours is from the lies and trifles of Porphyry, in which you exult as if they were divine voices, or from your *Misopogon* or *Antiochian* (for you subscribe both titles to that oration). What could be more shameful to Christians? At that time, the purple robes made it great, and everyone...

->PREFACE<-

...admiring flatterers: but now your beard is everywhere corrupted and plucked, and mocked along with its own authors. In this work, you boast greatly of your physical frugality and the fact that you never suffered from indigestion because you never overate, as if you were saying something truly marvelous. But you willingly overlook the fact that you so harshly expelled the Christians and held such a great and sacred people as nothing. Although one man might suffer from indigestion or emit natural belches, what harm does the Republic take from that? Yet when such a great persecution is stirred up, and such a great disturbance is brought upon the state, is it not absolutely necessary for Roman affairs to be in a wretched state? So much, then, for the *Misopogon* <note>The *Misopogon* (Beard-Hater) was a satirical work Julian wrote to mock the people of Antioch after they ridiculed his philosopher's beard and his austere lifestyle.</note>. 

After the winter had passed, Julian left Antioch to continue the expedition he had begun. When he reached Ctesiphon <note>The capital of the Sasanian Persian Empire.</note>, the most important city of the Persians, he perished from an uncertain wound in the thirty-second year of his life. He was Caesar for six years, and Augustus <note>Julian served first as a junior emperor (Caesar) under Constantius II, and later as the sole supreme ruler (Augustus).</note> for one year and five months. Furthermore, two oracles regarding his death are read in Suidas <note>The *Suda* (often referred to historically as Suidas) is a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the Mediterranean world.</note>, which I nonetheless believe to be a single one, though placed in reverse order <note>original Greek: *hysteron proteron* (ὕστερον πρότερον), a rhetorical device where the last thing is put first.</note>. Thus, I read in his work: *“There is also the oracle given to him when he was staying near Ctesiphon.”*

### CONCERNING THE DEATH
### The Oracle for Julian.

> Wise Zeus once devised a race of scepter-bearers,
> Most hateful to the blessed ones who hold Olympian homes.
> Julian, the god-like King of the Romans,
> Fighting the cities and the long walls of the Persians,
> Destroyed those who fight at close quarters with fierce fire and iron,
> And tirelessly subdued many cities and nations.
> But also, having taken the Alemannic soil of the Western men 
> With dense ranks, he laid waste to their fields.
> But when, with your scepters, you subdue the Persian blood
> With your swords, driving them as far as Seleucia,
> Then a fire-bright chariot shall lead you to Olympus,
> Whirled about in stormy eddies,
> After you have cast away the much-enduring pain of mortal habits;
> And you shall come to the ancestral hall of ethereal light,
> From which you wandered when you came into a mortal body.

That is to say: "There was indeed an oracle given to him while he was at Ctesiphon."

<meta>This page transitions from the technical comparison of manuscript variants to a more literary and moralizing conclusion regarding the life and death of the Emperor Julian. It concludes the commentary on his work "The Misopogon" (The Beard-Hater) with a poetic prophecy and a summary of his character.</meta>

# ON JULIAN’S “BEARD-HATER.”
<note>The *Misopogon* (Beard-Hater) was a satirical essay written by Emperor Julian in 363 AD, responding to the people of Antioch who had mocked his philosophical lifestyle and his beard.</note>

->The oracle concerning the death of Julian<-

> The wise Jupiter once destroyed the earth-born race,
> Who were most hostile to the blessed ones dwelling in celestial homes.
> The divine Julian, King of the Romans,
> Fighting, laid waste to the cities and long walls
> Of the warlike Persians with fire and hard iron,
> And bravely subdued many nations and cities.
> Furthermore, seizing the Alemannic soil of the Western men
> In frequent battles, he ravaged their fields.
> But after you have subdued the Persian blood with your swords,
> Shaking your scepters as far as Seleucia,
> Then a bright chariot, mixed with storms and whirlwinds on all sides,
> Shall carry you to heaven,
> Once the laborious care of mortal customs is cast aside.
> You shall come to the paternal mansion of ethereal light,
> From whence you came, migrating into a human body.
<note>This "oracle" reflects the Neo-Platonic belief held by Julian that his soul was a divine being sent to earth to restore order, destined to return to the stars after his death.</note>

For this reason, we have thus far the life of the Emperor Julian described and set forth. We have indeed observed the great praises of this prince in every kind of virtue; yet that supreme crime of apostasy <term>apostasias: the total desertion or departure from one's religion—in this case, Julian's rejection of Christianity for Paganism</term> arose from three causes: a fickleness of nature, a perversity of learning—especially in the magical arts—and finally, a lust for power. These brought upon him a most shameful stain and a most miserable end to his life. Therefore, if anyone considers this example diligently and accurately, they will indeed love and cultivate all virtues, but they will especially seek out piety as the foundation <term>krepida: from the Greek *krepis*, meaning a base, pedestal, or the sole of a shoe; the essential starting point</term> and groundwork of all virtues. Once it is known, they will hold fast to it and never allow themselves to be torn away from it.

# TO JULIAN
## THE EMPEROR.

> A great king of the Romans and a mighty warrior,
> Who excelled greatly in both actions and speech;
> Having been initiated into the lovely wisdom and sacred rites of Christ,
> He was ruined by turning away, and then persecuted those same things.
> It did not remain hidden, they say—and rightly so—what a conflicted mind
> He possessed; in the end, it was fully revealed.

->C. Martinos.<-

<note>original: "Γ. Μαρτίνος"</note>

<summary>This page presents a poetic "oracle" predicting Julian's death and divine ascent, followed by a moral summary that blames his downfall on his "apostasy" from Christianity despite his other virtues.</summary>

<keywords>Julian the Apostate, Misopogon, Oracle, Persia, Seleucia, Alemanni, Apostasy, Piety, C. Martinos</keywords>

# ON JULIAN’S "THE BEARD-HATER."
<note>The "Misopogon" (The Beard-Hater) was a satirical work written by Julian himself to mock the citizens of Antioch who had ridiculed his philosophical lifestyle and his beard.</note>

### An oracle concerning the death of Julian,

*Once the wise Jupiter destroyed the earth-born race,*
*The most bitter enemies to the blessed ones who dwell in celestial homes;*
*Julian, the divine King of the Romans,*
*Fighting, laid waste to the cities of the Persians and their long walls*
*With fire and hard iron, the tools of war,*
*And bravely subdued many cities and nations;*
*Furthermore, taking the Alemannic soil of the western men*
*In frequent battles, he ravaged their fields.*
*But after you have tamed the Persian blood with your scepter,*
*Striking with swords as far as Seleucia,*
*Then a bright chariot, mingled with storms and whirlwinds on every side,*
*Shall carry you into heaven,*
*Once the wearying care of mortal customs is cast aside;*
*You shall come to the paternal mansion of ethereal light,*
*From whence you migrated when you came into a human body.*
<note>This "oracle" frames Julian’s death not as a defeat, but as a divine homecoming, echoing the Neoplatonic belief that the soul descends from the stars and returns to them.</note>

For which reason, we have thus far described and set forth the life of Emperor Julian: We have certainly observed the great praises of that prince in every kind of virtue. However, that greatest crime of <term>impiety</term> <note>original Greek: asebeia</note> arose from three causes: a lightness of nature, a perversity of learning (especially in the magical arts), and finally, a greed for power. This brought upon him a most foul stain and a most wretched end to his life. Therefore, if anyone considers this example carefully and accurately, he will indeed love and cherish all virtues, but above all, he will seek out piety as the <term>base</term> <note>original Greek: krepida</note> and foundation of all virtues. Once known, he will hold it fast and never allow himself to be torn away from it.

---

# TO JULIAN
## the Emperor.

A great king of the Romans, and a mighty spearman,
   Excelling greatly in deeds as well as in words;
Initiated into the lovely wisdom and sacred rites of Christ,
   He perished by turning away, and persecuted those same things in turn.
He did not escape notice—for they say well—that whoever possessed
   A duplicitous mind, was entirely revealed at the end.

->G. Martinos.<-

*Wise Jupiter once destroyed the earth-born race,* <note>original: "Terrigenum quondam genus." This likely refers to the Giants of myth, who were enemies of the gods, here used as a metaphor for enemies of the divine order.</note>

For this reason, we have up to this point the life of Emperor Julian described and set forth: we have seen altogether great praises of that prince in every kind of virtue; nevertheless, that supreme crime of <term>apostasy</term> <note>original: "ἀποστασίας" (apostasias). Julian is famously known as "the Apostate" because he rejected Christianity in favor of traditional Roman paganism.</note> arising from three causes—fickleness of nature, perversity of doctrine especially in the magic arts, and finally a greed for power—brought upon him a most foul stain and a most miserable end of life. A technical term for the base or foundation of a building or a boot; used here metaphorically for the basis of all virtue.</note> and foundation of all virtues, and once it is known, will hold it tightly, nor ever allow himself to be torn from it.

# JULIAN THE EMPEROR’S
## MISOPOGON,
### *or The Antiochian.*

<margin>
1. This introduction <note>original: "Proœmium."</note> establishes the satire by contrasting certain poets with Julian: Anacreon played with varied songs; Alcaeus and Archilochus even took revenge on their enemies. Julian is permitted neither of these, yet he will do both in a way while using the Muses to reproach himself. The <term>protasis</term> <note>The first part of a formal rhetorical comparison or argument.</note> precedes this.
</margin>

<image-desc>An ornate woodcut initial 'A' featuring foliage and scrollwork.</image-desc>The poet Anacreon <note>A famous Greek lyric poet (c. 582–485 BC) known for his lighthearted poems on wine and love.</note> composed many songs that were both serious and charming, since the Muses gave him the ability to be playful. But to Alcaeus <note>A lyric poet from Lesbos often involved in political strife.</note> and Archilochus of Paros, <note>A poet legendary for his biting, aggressive lampoons.</note> God did not grant the Muses for the sake of pleasantry and pleasure. Instead, because they were forced to endure various injuries and troubles, they used their Muses for this purpose: they made the burdens that God <note>original: "Deus." Julian likely refers to the divine or fate in a general sense here.</note> had given them lighter through their own insults toward their enemies.

<margin>
2. The <term>antapodosis</term>. <note>The second part of a rhetorical comparison, where the speaker applies the preceding examples to their own specific situation.</note>
</margin>

But for me, the law forbids (as it does for all others, I believe) accusing by name those who, despite suffering no injury, nevertheless choose to be enemies of their own accord. Furthermore, the habits of my upbringing take away the music of poetry from me—a thing which is highly valued today among noble minds. For it seems shameful now to establish a musical style that has long been dedicated to the wealthy and the wicked.

<meta>This page continues Emperor Julian’s "Misopogon." On the previous page, Julian compared his own situation to the poets Anacreon, Alcaeus, and Archilochus. He picks up the thought here, explaining that while he lacks their poetic genius, he will still use writing to express his frustrations, even if his "song" is as unrefined as that of the barbarians he encountered during his military campaigns in Gaul.</meta>

# JULIAN THE EMPEROR’S

me; nonetheless, I will not, for that reason, abstain from the protection of the Muses so long as I am able. For indeed, I have seen those barbarians who dwell across the Rhine <note>Julian spent several years as a general in Gaul (modern France and Germany) fighting Germanic tribes before becoming Emperor.</note> zealously embrace and take delight in their own rustic songs, which are composed of words sounding much like the harsh cries emitted by birds. For it is common, I believe, for bad musicians to be unpleasant and annoying to those who hear them, even while they are naturally most pleasing to themselves. Therefore, when I considered this, I said to myself in silence and with great confidence: "Certainly, I shall sing for myself and for the Muses." 

<margin>
3. Thus far has been the introduction <note>original: "proœmium"</note>; what follows is the ironic criticism. The first chapter discusses the contempt for luxury and pleasures, first regarding his physical person, and then regarding his way of life. Concerning his person, there are the following: the length of his beard, the filth of his head, his nails, his fingers, and his entire body.
</margin>

This "song," however, is composed in prose <note>original: "soluta oratione," literally "loosened speech," the standard Latin term for prose as opposed to metered verse.</note> and contains many heavy insults—not, by Hercules, against others (for how could I do so, when the law prohibits it?), but against the poet and author himself. For no law forbids a man from writing praises or criticisms of himself. Indeed, if I wished to praise myself ever so much, I would not be able; but I shall be able to criticize myself in infinite ways.

# MISOPOGON

...his breathing was labored, and a deep flush spread across his face. When the doctor <note>original: "medicus" — referring to the famous physician Erasistratus.</note> observed this, he placed his hand upon the young man's chest; the heart was pounding violently, as if it were leaping from its proper place. He suffered in this way only in the presence of the Queen <note>Stratonice, his stepmother, with whom he was secretly in love.</note>. Yet, once she had left and the others followed, he became calm again, appearing just like anyone who feels no illness at all.

Having identified the "disease," Erasistratus explained the matter to the King. Because the King loved his children so dearly, he declared that he would give up his own wife to his son. At that time, the son refused; however, not long after his father’s death, he most greedily seized upon the very gift that he had previously—and quite nobly—rejected.

Such is the story of Antiochus <note>Julian refers here to Antiochus I Soter, the namesake of the city of Antioch.</note>. Therefore, it should cause no resentment if his descendants should imitate their grandfather, the founder of their race or at least the source of their name. For just as with plants, where qualities are likely to spread as widely as possible—and perhaps even produce offspring entirely identical to the source from which they grew—so too is it believable in humans that the character of the descendants is closely akin to that of their ancestors.

### THE BEARD-HATER (MISOPOGON)

...to share a bit of my own unpleasantness with everyone, so as not to completely wear out this happy city with the "stench" of my modesty and the self-restraint of my household.
