Even now, those who breed horses <term>equos alunt: refers to the 'hippotrophy,' the expensive duty of providing horses for public games</term> for you every year enjoy an exemption of three thousand acres <term>jugerum: a Roman measure of land, roughly 0.6 acres</term>, partly through the foresight and diligence of my uncle and namesake <note>Julian refers to his maternal uncle, Julian "the Count of the East," who served as a high official</note>, and partly through my own favor. 

Because I have punished thieves and imposters in this way, I naturally seem to you to be "turning the world upside down." For believe me, leniency <note>original: "lenitas"</note> and mercy <note>original: "clementia"</note> toward such people only nourishes and strengthens the wickedness of men.

<margin>Conclusion of the entire critique.</margin>
Therefore, my discourse now returns to the very point I intended. For I am the sole author of all my own misfortunes, since I bestowed my favors upon ungrateful souls. This should therefore be attributed to my own stupidity <note>original: "stultitiae"</note>, not to your "liberty" <note>Julian uses "libertati" sarcastically here to describe the unruly and disrespectful behavior of the Antiochenes</note>. Consequently, I shall strive to be more prudent and cautious among you in the future; and as for you, in return for the "honor" and "goodwill" which you have publicly shown me, may the gods grant you a fitting reward.

I had long supposed that you had already reached the Nile. Frequently calling to mind that which I am accustomed to say, I would remark: "O fortunate Egyptians, who have long possessed the Nile as the provider of all the goods it is known to bring." But I said they are now much more blessed, because they also enjoy your Muses <term>Muses: a classical metaphor for one's literary, philosophical, or artistic talents</term>, which are in no way inferior to the Nile, or—as I feel—are perhaps even greater. For while that river makes the people rich by irrigating their land, you, by stirring the minds of the youth with your speech, direct them toward the true riches of wisdom <note>original: "sapientiae"</note>, doing no less than Pythagoras did when he traveled to them, or Plato after him <note>Julian refers to the tradition that the great Greek philosophers Pythagoras and Plato traveled to Egypt to study ancient wisdom</note>. Therefore, I was discussing these things with myself in silence, while you, in the meantime, were not far away, though hidden from us. Thus, as soon as your letter was delivered to me, I was at first filled with wonder, and [suspected] it to be a trick...

### EMPEROR JULIAN

Even a few words are enough for you. You must know that many affairs of state are flowing in upon me from every side. ->To Libanius<-

## To Aristomenes the philosopher.

Must we really wait for a formal summons? Is the practice of always being the first to show regard to be found nowhere? Take care that we do not introduce this harsh rule of law, if we are to expect from friends only what we expect from strangers and casual acquaintances. One might be at a loss here and ask: "How can we be friends if we do not even know each other?" But then, how are we friends with those who lived a thousand—or by Zeus, even two thousand—years ago? It is because they were all men of excellence, and in their character they were "noble and good" <term>kaloi kagathoi</term> <note>original: "καλοί τε κἀγαθοί." Even if, as far as I am concerned, I fall quite short of actually being so, yet the desire itself somehow places us in their company. But why do I prattle on about such things at greater length?

THE EMPEROR JULIAN.

## To George.

"You have come, Telemachus," <note>original: "Ἦλθες Τηλέμαχε." Julian is quoting the Odyssey (16.23). In the epic, the swineherd Eumaeus greets Telemachus with these words; Julian uses the literary reference to express a warm, familiar welcome to his correspondent upon receiving a letter.</note> as the epic says. I too feel as if I have already seen you through your letters; I have received the impression of your sacred soul just as one receives the likeness of a large signet from a tiny seal. Indeed, it is possible for much to be revealed in a small space. 

Even the wise Phidias <note>Pheidias (c. 480–430 BCE) was the most famous sculptor of the Classical Greek world, known for his colossal "Chryselephantine" (gold and ivory) statues of Zeus at Olympia and Athena in the Parthenon.</note> was recognized not only for his statues at Olympia or Athens; he was also able to enclose the labor of a great art within a tiny engraving. They say he did this with his cicada, and his bee, and if you like, even his fly. Though each of these was cast in bronze by nature, each was given a soul <note>original: "enempsychōtai." To be "ensouled" or "animated," suggesting the art was so realistic it seemed to possess the breath of life.</note> by his art. Perhaps in those instances, the very smallness of the creatures themselves lent a natural fittingness to the scale of his craft. 

But consider instead, if you will, his Alexander <note>Alexander the Great. Julian is likely describing a famous engraved gem or a miniature relief sculpture depicting the Macedonian king.</note> hunting on horseback. The entire scene is no larger than a person’s fingernail. Yet it evokes such a sense of wonder at the art that the figure of Alexander appears to strike the beast and terrify the viewer, his intensity visible through his entire posture. Meanwhile, the horse stands on the very tips of its hooves...

## TO GEORGE.

<margin>George's eloquence is praised by a comparison of equals: Small works often reveal great masters; likewise, George's letters prove his own eloquence.</margin>
<margin>Regarding Phidias, see Pliny, Book 34, Chapter 8.</margin>
You know that verse: "You have come, my Telemachus." <note>original: "Venisti mi Telemache." This is a Latin rendering of the Greek "Ἦλθες, Τηλέμαχε" from Homer’s Odyssey (16.23). Julian uses the literary reference to express a warm, familiar welcome to his correspondent upon receiving a letter.</note> But I have already seen you in your letters, and I have grasped the image of your divine mind, just as if the likeness of some great statue <note>original: "signi." While it can mean a sign or mark, in this artistic context it refers to a large-scale statue.</note> had been impressed upon a tiny seal. Indeed, it is possible to reveal much in a small space.

That wise Phidias <note>Phidias (c. 480–430 BCE) was the most celebrated sculptor of ancient Greece, famous for his massive statues of Zeus at Olympia and Athena in the Parthenon.</note> was famous not only for those statues found in Olympia or Athens; he was also renowned because he could contain the labor of great art within a tiny sculpture. They say his cicada and his bee were like this—and if you like, his fly. Although nature formed each of these from bronze, art nevertheless adorned them with life and soul. <note>original: "vita atque anima." This reflects the Greek concept of *empsychos*, where a work of art is so realistic it appears to breathe.</note> Perhaps in those instances, the very smallness of the creatures lent a semblance of truth to the artist's diligence. 

But look, if you please, at his Alexander <note>Alexander the Great. Julian is describing a miniature work, likely an engraved gem or a small relief.</note> hunting from a horse. The size of the figure does not exceed the fingernail on a hand, and yet it is expressed with such wonderful artistry that Alexander actually strikes the beast and strikes terror into the viewer’s heart with his expression. Meanwhile, the horse seems to stand on the very tips of its hooves...

## JULIAN TO THE SAME.

The myth tells that the eagle, when he wishes to test the legitimacy of his offspring, carries them high into the upper air and brings them before the rays of the sun. ## JULIAN TO THE SAME.
<note>Addressing Maximus of Ephesus.</note>

<margin>Julian sends his writings to Maximus the philosopher to be corrected. This is a comparison of similarities.</margin>
The fables imagine that when the eagle wishes to test the legitimacy of its chicks, it carries them—still featherless and tender—high into the sky and exposes them to the rays of the sun <note>original: *solis*; the OCR likely misread the long 's' as an 'f'</note>. It is as if the bird calls upon God as a witness to separate the true father from the false and adulterous one. In the same way, we offer our writings to you as if to Mercury, the god of eloquence <term>Mercurius: the Roman name for Hermes, the god of speech, interpretation, and messenger of the gods</term>, so that if they can endure the test of your ears, you may decide at your own discretion whether they ought to fly out to the public. ->JULIANI IMP.<-

“Certainly,” I said, “that man will correct his writings; for up until now he has indeed been very immoderate.” Upon hearing this, he was so far from returning to sanity and modesty that he did things which no moderate tyrant would have done, especially since I was so near to him. But if something must be endured, it is no small consolation to depart with a right and upright conscience of mind. Would that the gods grant us Salutius <note>Saturninius Secundus Salutius, a high-ranking official and close, trusted friend of Julian known for his integrity and philosophical character</note>, an upright man.

## Julian to Eugenius the philosopher.

They say that Daedalus fashioned wings of wax for Icarius <note>original: "Ikariō"; Julian refers to the myth of Icarus, who fell into the sea when the sun melted his wings</note>, daring to force nature through art. For my part, while I praise his skill, I do not admire his judgment; for he alone was willing to entrust the safety of his child to melting wax. Instead, I would fly straight to the very foothills of your mountains, so that I might embrace you, "my darling"—as Sappho <note>Sappho was an influential female poet of the 7th century BCE; the phrase "my care" or "my darling" (Greek: *to melema toumon*) is a term of deep affection</note> says. ->LETTERS<-

And if perhaps a successor shall be given to us on this account, it will be, I hope, in no way troublesome. For a short span of time lived well and innocently is to be preferred to an immortality of wrongdoing. Peripatetic <term>Peripatetic: The school of philosophy founded by Aristotle, which emphasized empirical observation and practical ethics; the name derives from his habit of walking (peripatein) while teaching</term> philosophy is not, as some believe, more sluggish than the Stoic <term>Stoic: A school that taught that virtue is the only good and that one should remain indifferent to external circumstances and emotions</term>. However, in my opinion, this is the difference between the two: one is more passionate and turbulent, while the other is more prudent—namely, in its commitment to remaining steadfast in one's reasoned judgment.

### JULIAN TO EUSTOCHIUS

<margin>He invites a friend to the honor of the Consulship.</margin>
The wise **Hesiod** <note>A famous Greek poet of the 8th century BCE, known for his work "Works and Days," which contains practical advice on farming and social conduct.</note> believes that neighbors should be invited to feasts so that they may rejoice together, since when some disturbance or unexpected misfortune occurs, they also bear the common grief. ### Julian to Eustochius

The wise **Hesiod** <note>A Greek poet (c. 700 BCE) whose work *Works and Days* offers moral and practical advice.</note> thought it right to invite one's neighbors to feasts, so that they might share in the joy; for they also grieve and struggle alongside us whenever an unexpected trouble falls. ## JULIAN TO SARAPION
## *The Most Illustrious.*

<margin>He sends a certain friend one hundred Damascus figs: from this, a praise of the fig and of the number one hundred is woven.</margin>
Different people are accustomed to sending different sorts of tributes; but I send to you one hundred of our local long dried figs <note>original: "caricas" — a term for dried figs, originally associated with Caria in Asia Minor.</note>, which you will receive as a pleasant token of sweet banquets. Thus, from one comes ten, and from these—by returning into themselves—one hundred are procreated. ## JULIAN TO THE JEWS
### *To the Community, if this letter is authentic.* <note>original: "Reipub. si vera est." This subtitle likely reflects a later editor's note regarding the long-standing scholarly debate over whether Julian actually wrote this letter or if it was a later forgery.</note>

<margin>
He remits certain taxes to the Jews.
</margin>
Past times were not so much troublesome for you on account of your servitude, but rather because you were subject to tax assessments <note>original: "tabulis." Literally "tablets" or "account books," referring to official tax registers.</note> issued without the emperor’s command, and were forced to bring vast amounts of gold into the treasury <note>original: "ærarium." Furthermore, I have prohibited a tax that was already being prepared against you once again; I have suppressed this detestable wickedness <note>original: "impietatem." Impiety or lack of duty; here Julian uses it to describe the previous administration's unfair treatment.</note> and burned the records that were stored in my archives <note>original: "scriniis." Desks or cases for keeping scrolls and documents.</note> for the purpose of oppressing you, so that no one may henceforth be permitted to spread the report of such great impiety against you. And indeed, the blame for these wrongs should not be attributed to my brother **Constantius** <note>original: "Constantio." Constantius II (r. 337–361 AD), Julian’s predecessor and cousin. Julian formally calls him "brother" here as was imperial custom, despite their historical rivalry.</note>, a man worthy of memory, but rather to certain men who were barbaric in soul and impious in mind...

### JULIAN’S LAW CONCERNING *physicians.*

Experience itself demonstrates that the medical art is beneficial to mankind. Therefore, philosophers—not without reason—proclaim that it descended from heaven. For the weakness of our nature, and the disturbances of health <note>original: "valetudinis offensiones," referring to illnesses or physical setbacks.</note> which occur daily, are corrected through this art. Therefore, just as the principle of fairness demands, and following the authority and voice of previous rulers, we command out of our own humanity that you shall live free from **Senatorial duties** <term>Senatoriis muneribus (heavy financial and administrative obligations imposed on the wealthy classes to fund local government)</term> for the future.

### Decree to the Alexandrians.

It was only right that one who was driven out by so many
imperial decrees of many emperors, should have waited for
a legal imperial command before returning to his own country,
instead of acting with such audacity and madness, as if
offending the laws as though they did not exist.
For even now, although we granted the **Galileans** <note>original: "Γαλιλαίοις." This was Julian’s preferred derogatory name for Christians, intended to emphasize their origins as a local provincial sect rather than a universal religion.</note> who were

it was not to their churches that we granted their return,
but to their own homelands. Yet I hear that **Athanasius** <note>original: "Αθανασίον." Athanasius of Alexandria was a powerful bishop and a major opponent of Arianism. Julian viewed him as a dangerous political agitator.</note>,
that most daring man, raised up by his usual insolence,
has seized what is called among them the **episcopal throne** <note>original: "ἐπισκοπῆς θρόνου." The bishop's seat or office.</note>.
This, I know, is not moderately unpleasant to the god-fearing
people of Alexandria.
Therefore, we publicly command him to depart from the city on the
very day he receives the letter of our **Clemency** <term>ἡμερότητος (Clemency/Mildness). This was a formal title used by Roman Emperors to describe their own administrative grace or person, regardless of how harsh the actual command might be.</term>;
and if he remains within the city, we warn him of much
greater and more severe punishments.

<margin>
On the exile

It was only right that he who had been cast out by several royal and imperial edicts should have at least waited for a single royal edict before returning home, instead of relying on exceptional audacity and madness to mock the laws as if they were entirely extinguished and ruined. Indeed, this is no small displeasure to the people of Alexandria. Therefore, we command him to leave the city on the very day he receives this letter of our **Humanity** <term>humanitatis nostræ (Our Humanity): A formal imperial title used to describe the Emperor’s administrative grace or mildness, even when issuing a harsh decree.</term>; but if he remains in the city, we declare far greater and more severe punishments for him.

### Julian to Aetius, Bishop.

To all others who were in any way exiled by the late Constantius <note>Constantius II, Julian’s predecessor and cousin, who was a devout Arian Christian and often banished theological opponents</note> because of the "madness of the Galilaeans," <note>original: "τῆς τῶν Γαλιλαίων ἀπονοίας"; Julian used the term 'Galilaeans' to dismissively refer to Christians, suggesting they were merely a local sect from Galilee rather than a world religion</note> I have remitted their sentence of exile. ### Julian to Lucian, Sophist.

### Julian to Dositheus.

## Julian to Iamblichus the Philosopher.

It was enough for Odysseus, when he was checking his son’s false impression of him, to say:
<margin>Odyssey, Book 16</margin> "I am no god; why do you liken me to the immortals?" <note>original: "Οὔτοι τις θεός εἰμι· τί μ’ ἀθανάτοισιν ἐΐσκεις;"; Julian quotes Homer’s Odyssey 16.187, where Odysseus reveals himself to his son Telemachus, who had mistaken his father for a deity</note> 
But as for me, I would say that I am barely even a man—as the saying goes—so long as I am not in the company of Iamblichus. <note>Iamblichus of Chalcis (c. 245–325 AD) was a Syrian Neoplatonist philosopher. Julian considered him the pinnacle of wisdom, though Iamblichus had actually died several decades before Julian became emperor</note> However, I confess that I am a devotee <note>original: "ἐραστὴς" (erastes); in the Platonic tradition, this refers to a "lover of wisdom" or a person driven by intense intellectual and spiritual affection</note> of yours, just as that father was of Telemachus. For even if you call me unworthy, not even that will deprive me of my longing for you. 

Since I have heard that many have become "lovers" of beautiful statues, not only doing no harm to the creator's skill, but even adding a living pleasure to the work through their passion for it. As for those ancient and wise men, with whom you playfully wish to compare me, I would say that I am as far from them as I believe I am from the number of students who attend your school. And yet you compare me not only to Pindar, <note>A famous Greek lyric poet known for his odes</note> nor Democritus, <note>An Ancient Greek philosopher known for the atomic theory of the universe</note> nor Orpheus the most ancient, <note>The mythical musician and prophet; Julian refers to him as a historical source of ancient theology</note> but to the whole of the Greek world together—at least as many as are remembered for reaching the summit of <term>philosophy: here meaning the combined pursuit of wisdom, science, and theology</term>—as if they were the various [notes] <note>original: "φθόγγων" (phthongon), which appears as the catchword for the next page; the metaphor describes these great thinkers as individual strings or notes forming a single harmonious lyre</note> of a lyre...

<note>original: "JULIANI IMP." — Flavius Claudius Julianus, the Roman Emperor (reigned 361–363 AD) who sought to revive traditional Greek religion and culture.</note>

->“One man yet, somewhere alive, is held back in the wide world.”<-
<note>A quote from Homer’s *Odyssey* (4.498). In the original poem, it refers to Odysseus being alive but trapped on an island; here, Julian uses it to suggest that Iamblichus is the last living link to the greatness of the ancient world.</note>

### The Emperor Julian to Porphyrius, greetings.

There was a very large and extensive library belonging to George <note>George of Cappadocia, the Arian Christian bishop of Alexandria who was lynched by a mob in 361 AD. ### TO AMERIUS.

<margin>He consoles Amerius on the death of his wife, using the example of Darius.</margin>

I read your letter not without tears, in which you write of the death of your wife and describe the bitterness of the misfortune. For while the matter is mournful in itself—that a wife, young and chaste, and a joy to her husband, and moreover the mother of excellent children, was snatched away before her time, like a torch lit and shortly after extinguished—it is truly very painful to me that this grief has fallen upon you. Indeed, our Amerius was the most undeserving of all men to taste any trouble or grief, being a man of excellent eloquence <note>original Latin: "oratione optimus." This likely refers to Amerius's reputation as a rhetorician or philosopher; Amerius was a known student of the Neoplatonist Porphyry.</note> and most closely joined to us in friendship. But indeed, if I were writing to someone else, I would certainly need a much longer discourse to teach him both that such a misfortune is a part of being human, and that it is necessary to bear it; and that in a heavier mourning there is no greater consolation; finally, I would apply all the remedies that seem fit for soothing grief, as if to one inexperienced in such matters. But as it is, since it seems shameful <note>Julian is about to argue that Amerius is too wise and philosophically trained to need the basic consolations offered to common people. The text breaks off here and continues on the next page.</note>

## TO AMERIUS.

I read your letter not without tears, in which you wrote concerning the death of your wife, reporting the extreme nature of your suffering. For besides being a cause of grief in its own right—that a woman, young and virtuous and beloved by her husband, and moreover the mother of noble <note>original: "ἱερῶν," literally "sacred" or "holy," here used as an epithet for children of high character.</note> children, should be snatched away before her time like a burning torch that soon after extinguishes its flame—the fact that this suffering extends to you seems to me no less painful. For our excellent Amerius was the least deserving of all men to undergo such a painful experience, being a man of noble character in speech <note>original Greek: "λόγῳ χρηστὸς." This refers to both Amerius's eloquence as a scholar and his moral integrity.</note> and the most cherished of all our friends. Nevertheless, if I were writing to anyone else on these matters, I would have certainly thought a longer discourse necessary—pointing out that what happened is merely part of the human condition, that it must be borne as a necessity, and that excessive grieving yields no further benefit—applying all the remedies that seem fitting for the consolation of such suffering, as though instructing someone who did not know better. But since I consider it quite shameful <note>Julian is suggesting that for a man of Amerius's philosophical stature, such common platitudes would be an insult to his intelligence and training.</note>

->### EMPEROR JULIAN ###<-

We consider **right education** <note>original: *paideian orthên*. *Paideia* refers to the entire system of Greek education, culture, and character-formation.</note> to be not merely the mastery of words, nor the expensive harmony of the tongue, but a **healthy disposition** of a mind that possesses intelligence, along with true opinions about what is good and evil, and what is beautiful and shameful. Whoever, then, thinks one thing but teaches another to those who approach him <note>Referring to his students.</note> seems to be as far removed from education as he is from being an honest man. 

And if the difference between one’s conviction and one’s tongue were over trivial matters, such a person would be bad only in that regard, and it would be a matter of degree. But if in the greatest matters one thinks one thing and teaches the opposite of what he believes, how is this not the behavior of **peddlers** <note>original: *kapêlôn*. A derogatory term for small-scale retailers, often used by philosophers to describe those who "sell" knowledge for profit without caring for its truth.</note>—not of honest men, but of the most wicked? 

They teach exactly what they believe to be most worthless, deceiving and baiting with praise those to whom they wish, I believe, to transfer their own evils. Therefore, it is necessary for all who profess to teach anything at all to be upright in character, and not to carry opinions in their souls that conflict with those they **publicly present**; <note>original: *metacharaktêrizontas*. Literally "re-stamping" or "re-minting," like a coin being given a different face than its true metal suggests.</note> but much

But especially those who instruct youth in the writings of the ancients ought to be such [upright] men, whether they are **Rhetoricians**, or **Grammarians**, and especially **Sophists** <note>original: *Sophiſtæ*. I desire both your ears and your tongue (as you yourselves would say) to be reborn in those matters—of which I pray I may always be a participant, along with all those who love me. # LETTERS.

I desire both your ears—as you yourselves would say—and your tongue to be reborn <note>original: *exanagennēthēnai*. Julian is likely mocking the Christian concept of being "born again," suggesting instead a "rebirth" into the classical Greek tradition.</note> in those matters in which I pray I may always participate, along with whoever is a friend to me in thought and in deed. For leaders and teachers, this common law is established: any of the young men who wish to attend school is not barred. For it would be entirely irrational to shut out boys from the best path while they are still ignorant of which way they should turn, or to drive them toward their ancestral customs <note>original: *patria*. Here referring to the traditional Roman and Greek religion that Julian sought to restore.</note> through fear and against their will. Although it would actually be just to heal such people against their will, as one does with those suffering from madness; nevertheless, let there be an allowance for everyone to suffer from such a disease. For I believe we should teach, rather than punish, those who are mindless.

If any mistake has been made, do not investigate it too severely, nor as one rhetorician against another. <note>Julian here concludes his personal letter to Evagrius, asking him to overlook any stylistic flaws in his writing with the grace of a friend rather than the scrutiny of a professional orator.</note>

<margin>He remits part of the tax debts.</margin>
To a King looking only for profit, your request would seem difficult; nor would he ever allow harm to be done to the public **revenues** <term>vectigalia: the general term for state incomes, including customs duties and rents.</term> for the sake of a few people. But because our intention is not to collect as much as possible from our subjects, but to benefit them as much as possible: for that reason, we grant you a pardon for your debts. Yet not all of them; rather, one part shall be granted to you, and the other shall go to the soldiers—which indeed will itself be largely for your own benefit, especially since it is spent for the sake of your peace and security. Therefore, we remit to you whatever is outstanding from past times up to the **third tribute** <note>original: "tertium tributum". I have written to the **prefects** <term>praefectos: high-ranking civil administrators responsible for tax collection and regional governance.</term> regarding this matter, so that the favor granted to you in word may be fulfilled in deed.

# TO ARSACIUS, THE HIGH PRIEST

->Letter of King Julian <note>The Greek "basileōs" is translated here as "King," though in the Roman context it refers to his title as Emperor.</note> to Galatia.<-

**Hellenism** <note>The term Julian used for the traditional Greek religious system he sought to restore in place of Christianity.</note> is not yet prospering according to our wishes, because of those who practice it. Yet the works of the gods are brilliant and great, surpassing every prayer and every hope. May **Adrasteia** <note>original: "Ἀδράστεια." Another name for Nemesis, the goddess of retribution. Julian invokes her here to avoid the appearance of pride when speaking of his success.</note> be merciful to our words. For who, a short time ago, would have dared to hope for such a great change in so little time? 

Why then do we think this is enough, and do not look at what has most increased the "godlessness" <note>Julian ironically uses the term "godlessness" to describe Christianity, which he viewed as a betrayal of the ancient gods.</note> of the rivals—their **philanthropy** <term>Philanthropy</term> <note>From the Greek 'philanthrōpia,' meaning 'love of humanity.' Julian notes that Christian charity was a key factor in their growth.</note> toward strangers, their care for the burial of the dead, and their feigned holiness of life? Each of these things I believe we ourselves ought truly to practice. 

And it is not enough for you alone to be such a person, but absolutely all the priests throughout **Galatia** <note>A region in central Anatolia, modern-day Turkey.</note> must be so. You must either shame them or persuade them <gloss>to</gloss> <gloss>be</gloss> <gloss>diligent</gloss>-diligent <note>The glosses here assist in reconstructing the Greek word 'spoudaioi,' meaning earnest or virtuous.</note>, or else remove them from the priestly service, if they do not approach the gods together with their wives, children, and servants, but instead tolerate their own household members—whether servants, sons, or **Galilean** <note>Julian’s preferred derogatory name for Christians.</note> wives—behaving impiously toward the gods and preferring "godlessness" to piety.

## LETTER OF THE EMPEROR JULIAN
### addressed to Arsacius, the High Priest of Galatia.

*The reason that the religion of the Gentiles* <note>original: "religio Gentilium." This refers to the traditional Greco-Roman polytheism Julian sought to restore.</note> *does not yet prosper according to our intention is due to those who profess it. However, the gifts the gods have granted us are splendid, great, and more excellent than anyone could have even prayed for or hoped for. For in so short a span of time—may **Nemesis** <note>original: "Nemesis." The goddess of retribution; Julian invokes her to avoid "divine jealousy" for boasting of his success.</note> be favorable to our words—hardly anyone would have dared to hope for such a significant change in affairs a short while ago. But why do we think this is enough, as if nothing more were needed, and do not instead turn our eyes to those things by which the impious religion of the Christians has grown? That is, their kindness toward strangers, the care they show in burying the dead, and the holiness of life they feign? Each of these things, I believe, must be truly practiced by us.*

*And it is not enough for this practice alone to be observed with sanctity; but I would have you either drive by threats or persuade by reason all our priests who inhabit **Galatia** <note>A region in central Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey).</note> to be honorable. Otherwise, remove them from the priestly office if they do not, together with their wives, children, and servants, attend diligently to the worship of the gods. Do not allow them to permit their servants, sons, or spouses of the **Galileans** <term>Galileans</term> <note>Julian’s derogatory term for Christians, used to imply they were merely a provincial sect rather than a universal religion.</note> to impiously*

## Julian to the Alexandrians.

If the founder of your city had been one of those few who, having transgressed their own law, revolted—choosing to live lawlessly and introducing a novel proclamation and teaching—it would still not be reasonable for **Athanasius** <note>Athanasius (c. 296–373 AD) was the Bishop of Alexandria and a chief defender of Trinitarianism. Julian, a staunch pagan, viewed him as a dangerous agitator and exiled him multiple times.</note> to be sought after by you. But as it is, since **Alexander** was the founder of your city, and since your presiding deity is **Lord Serapis** <note>original: "Σαράπιδος" (Sarapidos). Serapis was a Graeco-Egyptian deity promoted by the Ptolemies as a patron of Alexandria, combining traits of Osiris, Apis, and Zeus.</note>, together with his consort, the **Maiden** <note>Likely referring to Persephone or a Hellenized form of a local goddess associated with the cult of Serapis.</note>, and **Isis**, the Queen of all Egypt—you do not emulate the healthy part of the city. Instead, the diseased part <note>Julian frequently uses medical metaphors, characterizing paganism as "healthy" and Christianity as a "disease" or "infection."</note> dares to arrogate to itself the name of the "city." 

By the gods, men of Alexandria, I am deeply ashamed if any Alexandrian at all confesses to be a **Galilean** <term>Galilean: Julian's preferred derogatory term for Christians, intended to emphasize their origins as a provincial Jewish sect rather than a universal religion</term>. The ancestors of the true **Hebrews** were slaves to the **Egyptians** long ago. But now, you men of Alexandria—having conquered the Egyptians, for your founder conquered Egypt—subject yourselves to a **voluntary slavery** to a doctrine that scorns ancestral traditions, standing in direct opposition to the ancient laws. And it does not enter— <note>The text breaks off here; the catchword "ται" (tai) indicates the next page begins with the completion of the verb "εἰσέρχεται" (it enters).</note>

<summary>Emperor Julian scolds the citizens of Alexandria for embracing Christianity, arguing that as a city founded by Alexander the Great and protected by Serapis, they should reject the "disease" of the Galileans.</summary>

### THE LETTERS OF EMPEROR JULIAN

...those who have been led astray. For one must persuade by reason and teach men, not by blows, nor insults, nor bodily torture. Once again and many times I urge those who are zealous for the true worship of the gods <term>theosébeia: literally "god-reverence," referring here to the traditional Roman and Greek religion</term> not to wrong the crowds of the Galilaeans <note>Julian’s derogatory term for Christians, intended to emphasize their provincial origin.</note>, nor to attack them, nor to insult them. Julian views the abandonment of the ancient gods as a form of social and spiritual disease.</note>. And it happens that those who have turned away from the gods toward the dead and their relics <note>A disparaging reference to the Christian practice of venerating the remains of martyrs.</note> pay this very price. For we suffer along with those who are afflicted by a disease, but we rejoice with those who are being released and set free by the gods.

It has been no short time since I was staying <gloss>\* \*</gloss> in the West <note>original: "Hesperia." This refers to Julian’s time in Gaul (modern France) between 355-361 AD.</note>, when, after I learned that you pleased him <note>Likely referring to a shared acquaintance or perhaps the previous Emperor, though Julian often speaks in riddles about his time under Constantius II.</note> greatly, I called you my friend. And to do <gloss>\*</gloss> that well is my custom, out of a certain political caution <term>eulabeia: a sense of "prudence" or "discretion," often used by Julian to describe his careful navigation of the imperial court before he became sole Emperor</term>. For I did not... <gloss>\*</gloss> nor did I see how one ought to consider knowledge to be the guide of friendship, and experience to be the guide of knowledge. But, as it seems, a certain reputation—and not the least—was held by me, as you yourself said; because of which I thought back then that I should enroll you among my acquaintances. And now I look upon a matter that is dear to me, and most profitable to all people everywhere. May you handle it well, as it was worthy to hope you would, providing much gladness here <note>Referring to the present world or the specific region of Asia Minor where Theodorus was appointed.</note>, and providing a greater, good hope for the future. For we are certainly not among those convinced that souls either perish before their bodies or perish along with them; rather, we believe no man, but only the gods, whom it is most likely alone know these things—if indeed one should call "likely" that which is necessary. For it is fitting for men to guess about such matters, but for the gods to truly know them...

# LETTERS.

->JULIAN THE EMPEROR<-

...the gods, it is necessary. What then is this? <gloss>\*</gloss> I say to you now that you are to oversee, as the head of all the temples throughout Asia <note>original: "Asia." This refers specifically to the Roman province of Asia in western Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey), not the entire continent.</note>, <gloss>\*</gloss> the city, and to assign <gloss>\*</gloss> what is appropriate to each. First and foremost, what is proper for a ruler is goodness, and along with it, philanthropy <term>philanthropia: literally "love of mankind." Julian promoted this as a core Hellenic virtue, urging his priests to engage in social welfare to rival the growing influence of Christian charity</term> toward those who are worthy of receiving it. For whoever is unjust toward men is lawless toward the gods; and he who is insolent toward everyone must either be taught with frankness <term>parrhesia: the Greek tradition of "bold speech" or "candid speech," often used in a philosophical or political context</term> or must be punished with severity. 

Now, as for those things that must be organized in common for all the temples more completely, they will be issued very soon along with the rest; but for the time being, I wish to suggest a few things, and it is right that you should follow my guidance in such matters. For indeed, I do not improvise most of these things—as all the gods know—but if anyone is, I am cautious <term>eulabes: a term meaning both "pious" and "circumspect." Julian often uses it to describe his religious devotion</term> and I avoid innovation <term>kainotomia: literally "cutting new paths." Julian used this word as a pejorative to describe what he saw as the "novelty" of Christianity compared to the ancient traditions of Rome and Greece</term> in almost everything, one might say, and especially in matters regarding the gods. For I believe it is necessary to guard the ancestral laws from the beginning <gloss>\* \*</gloss>, which it is clear the gods gave. For they would not have been so beautiful had they merely originated from men. It happen...

<meta>This page continues Emperor Julian’s instruction to the High Priest Theodorus. In the preceding text, Julian warned against "innovation" and called for a return to ancient religious rigor. Here, he contrasts the lukewarm devotion of his fellow Hellenes (pagans) with the strict adherence to dietary laws seen in Judaism, which he uses as a model for the level of piety he expects from his priesthood.</meta>

# LETTERS.

->JULIAN THE EMPEROR<-

...but having allowed them to be neglected and corrupted, since wealth and luxury have prevailed, I think it is necessary to take care of such matters as if they were in a state of revolt. For I see that there is much negligence among us toward the gods, and that piety <term>eusebeia: the traditional sense of duty, reverence, and religious devotion to the gods</term> toward the higher powers has been driven out by impure luxury. 

I have always lamented these things within myself. [I observe] those who hold to a virtuous piety <note>original: "eusebeias chrestes." Julian is referring to the Jews. Though he disagreed with their exclusive monotheism, he deeply admired their dedication to ancient, ancestral laws, which contrasted with the "new" religion of Christianity.</note> to be so ardent that they choose for its sake to endure every want and famine, rather than taste pork or anything that has not been properly drained <note>original: "me apothlibentos." Literally "not squeezed out." This refers to the Jewish practice of ritual slaughter (shechita) to ensure blood is removed from the meat.</note>. Yet we are so indifferent toward the laws established for the gods that we have forgotten our ancestral customs <term>patrion: the traditional, "father-inherited" ways of the Greeks which Julian sought to restore against modern changes</term>. We are now even ignorant of whether such things were ever commanded at all. 

Yet those men [the Jews] are in their own way worshippers of God <note>original: "theosebeis." A term meaning "God-fearing" or "pious."</note>, since the one they honor is truly most powerful and most good, and he governs the sensible world <term>aistheton kosmon: the physical, visible universe perceived by the senses, as opposed to the intellectual or spiritual realm</term>. Indeed, I know well that we too worship Him under other names. They seem to me to act reasonably, those who do not trans- <note>The text cuts off mid-word; likely "transgress" (parabainontes).</note>

<summary>Emperor Julian criticizes the spiritual apathy and "luxury" of his fellow pagans, contrasting it with the strict religious discipline and dietary laws of the Jews. He acknowledges the Jewish God as a powerful deity who governs the physical world, asserting that the Greeks worship the same power under different names.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the fragment of Julian’s letter to the High Priest Theodorus. Building on the previous page's admiration for Jewish ritual strictness, Julian now clarifies his theological disagreement with them before pivoting to a harsh critique of the Christians, whom he views as a corrupted offshoot of Judaism.</meta>

# LETTERS.

### LETTERS OF EMPEROR JULIAN

...they seem to err in this one respect only: that they do not also worship the other gods, who are pleasing to that Supreme God <note>original: "to malista to theo." Literally "the greatest God." Julian, a Neoplatonist, identifies the God of the Jews with the supreme Creator or "the One," but argues that this supreme being is served by many subordinate deities whom the Jews wrongly ignore.</note> whom they serve. But those others <note>Julian here shifts his focus from the Jews to the Christians, whom he famously and derogatorily dubbed "the Galileans."</note> think that we, the nations <term>ethnesin: the "nations" or Gentiles; in this context, Julian refers to the Greeks and Romans who follow the traditional polytheistic religions</term>, are alone excluded [from the truth]. They themselves, having been raised up to this state of madness by a barbaric arrogance <note>original: "alazoneia barbarike." Julian frequently contrasted "Greek" reason and culture with what he saw as the "barbaric" (foreign and irrational) nature of Christian doctrine.</note>, those impious men from Galilee, have introduced their own way of life like a pestilence <term>nosema: a disease or plague; a recurring metaphor Julian used to describe the rapid spread of Christianity, which he viewed as a social and religious infection</term> upon the world.
